headline: Roosters win the NRL Grand Final by one point, US midterms deliver a Democratic sweep, and your ASX holdings slip on a soft local session while US tech held up last night.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS tracks the entire US share market, and today's ASX-priced unit fell 2.7% — largely reflecting the AUD/USD exchange rate drop (the Aussie fell about 0.9 cents overnight) and last night's US session being priced in. The underlying US market actually rose last night, so this is partly a currency translation effect. Long-term story unchanged.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: The AI-focused ETF slid 2.7% today in a broad ASX pullback. No specific fund news drove this — it's tracking weakness in global tech sentiment on the local exchange. Worth noting this holding is down 20% overall, reflecting how volatile the AI theme has been. Long-term AI tailwinds remain real, but expect continued bumps.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG slipped 1.6% today as the ASX 200 finished down 0.5% and global growth assets softened. As a diversified fund with heavy international exposure, the weaker Aussie dollar adds some drag on days like this. Nothing structural — this is normal session-to-session noise for a high-growth diversified fund.

movers.name: BetaShares Diversified All Growth ETF
movers.note: DHHF dropped 1.5% in today's ASX session, moving in line with the broader market dip. No specific news. As a 100% growth-focused diversified ETF, it tends to feel soft sessions a bit more than balanced funds. Long-term thesis intact.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: A bright spot today — VGE rose 1.2% on the ASX, bucking the broader market weakness. Emerging markets got a small lift as the US midterm Democratic sweep raised hopes for a more multilateral trade stance, which tends to benefit developing economies. Good day for this holding.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara was flat today at $2.83 — no movement, no news. The lithium market remains subdued and the stock is still well below its peak. No new catalysts today, positive or negative.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two edged up 0.7% last night on the NASDAQ — and there's good reason for optimism. GTA 6 preorder sales reportedly hit $751 million with two weeks still to go before release, and new screenshots are generating serious buzz about the game's graphics quality. A physical edition leak also surfaced. The GTA 6 launch is shaping up as a massive event for the company.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google rose 0.8% last night. Some analyst commentary questioned whether core Search is under pressure, but the headline numbers remain solid. There's also debate about Alphabet's $15 billion Malaysia data centre investment — some see it as AI overreach, others as essential infrastructure. Last night's move suggests the market is shrugging off the noise for now.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dipped about 1% last night despite the broader NASDAQ rising over 1%. With Democrats now controlling Congress, there's growing chatter about tighter tech regulation, and Microsoft — as one of the biggest AI players — could face more scrutiny. Short-term pressure, but the long-term AI story for Microsoft remains very strong.

watch_today.title: GTA 6 preorders hit $751M — big moment for TTWO
watch_today.detail: With two weeks until release, GTA 6 preorder sales have reportedly hit $751 million. New screenshots are generating massive hype around graphics quality, and a physical edition leak has only added to the buzz. This is shaping up as one of the biggest game launches in history. For a long-term holder, this is exactly the moment you've been waiting for — the thesis is playing out.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX down 2.7% today — still holding the AI theme
watch_today.detail: The AI ETF slid again today, and the overall position is now down about 20% from your cost base. No specific bad news today — it's broad market drag and AI sector volatility. The long-term case for AI as a transformative technology is intact, and this ETF gives diversified exposure to that theme. Sit tight unless your risk tolerance has changed.

watch_today.title: VTS.AX fell 2.7% — but the US market actually rose last night
watch_today.detail: VTS dropped sharply on the ASX today, but don't be alarmed — the underlying US market (NASDAQ up 1.1%, S&P up 0.3%) actually did well last night. The fall in VTS is mainly a currency effect: the Aussie dollar dropped about 0.9 cents overnight, which inflates the apparent AUD price drop when the fund is revalued. Your US exposure is in good shape.

watch_today.title: Democrats sweep US midterms — watch for tech regulation risk
watch_today.detail: The Democratic Party has won control of both houses of Congress in the US midterms. They've flagged plans for AI regulation legislation and are expected to push harder on big tech. Microsoft and Alphabet (Google) are both in your portfolio and could face more regulatory scrutiny over the next two years. Worth monitoring, but not a reason to sell — regulation rarely kills these businesses, it just adds friction.

watch_today.title: Iran war risk staying elevated despite US election result
watch_today.detail: CNBC and multiple outlets are reporting that despite the Democratic midterm sweep, the risk of escalation in the Iran conflict remains high. Oil is sitting around $90.83/barrel — elevated by historical standards. If the conflict widens, oil could spike further, which flows through to inflation and potentially higher interest rates globally. Keep an eye on this as a macro risk.

watch_today.title: RBA cash rate at 4.85% — mortgage pressure ongoing
watch_today.detail: Australia's cash rate has hit 4.85%, with CBA, NAB, Westpac and ANZ all passing on the increase. This keeps pressure on household budgets and consumer spending, which flows through to ASX-listed companies. No immediate action needed for your portfolio, but it's a headwind for the broader Australian economy and local equities.

world.summary: The big story globally is the US midterm elections delivering a Democratic sweep, while the Iran conflict continues to simmer and Israel undergoes a political shake-up. Gold dropped and oil held steady.

stories.title: Democrats win control of US Congress in midterm elections
stories.why_it_matters: The Democratic Party has swept the 2026 US midterm elections, winning control of both the House and Senate. The Guardian describes it as voters 'roundly rejecting' Trump's alternate reality. Democrats are now planning legislation on healthcare, tariffs and artificial intelligence regulation — but have explicitly ruled out pursuing Trump impeachment. For markets, the shift means more regulatory pressure on big tech and potentially a softer stance on trade tariffs, which is mixed news for US equities.

stories.title: Iran war risk remains high despite Democratic election win
stories.why_it_matters: Despite hopes that a Democratic win might ease tensions, analysts at CNBC say the risk of the Iran conflict escalating remains very high. The situation involves the US, Israel, and Iran's ability to threaten the Strait of Hormuz — the world's most important oil shipping lane. If that strait is disrupted, global oil prices could spike dramatically, pushing up petrol prices and inflation worldwide. Oil is already sitting at around $90.83 a barrel.

stories.title: Israel President invites Gadi Eisenkot to form new government
stories.why_it_matters: Israel's President has invited Gadi Eisenkot — a former military chief and current opposition figure — to attempt to form a new government. This signals a significant political shift in Israel amid the ongoing regional conflict. A change in Israeli leadership could affect how aggressively the country pursues military operations and how willing it is to pursue diplomatic solutions. The situation remains fluid and bears watching.

stories.title: Global travel set to hit record levels in 2026 despite Middle East conflict
stories.why_it_matters: Despite ongoing conflict in the Middle East, global travel is on track for record-breaking numbers in 2026 according to The Independent. Consumer appetite for international holidays has remained remarkably resilient. This is good news for airlines, hotels, and tourism-related businesses globally — and suggests the broader consumer economy is holding up better than some feared.

stories.title: Paraguay's ousted president charged over major bank collapse
stories.why_it_matters: Paraguay's former president has been formally charged with crimes linked to the collapse of a major Paraguayan bank. The case highlights ongoing governance and corruption risks across Latin America — a region that includes several emerging market economies. For anyone with emerging markets exposure (like VGE.AX), this is a reminder of the political risk baked into these investments, though Paraguay is a small part of any EM index.

markets.summary: Last night the NASDAQ jumped over 1% and the S&P 500 edged up 0.3% as the US midterm results came in and markets responded positively to the Democratic sweep. The ASX 200 finished down 0.5% today. The Aussie dollar weakened, gold fell, and oil was broadly flat.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: ASX finished down 0.5% today — a mild pullback with no single dominant driver.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session saw a modest gain as midterm results came in — markets like the certainty of an election result.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech stocks surged over 1% last night on the NASDAQ — a strong night for the index.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar slipped about 0.9 cents — this drags on the AUD value of your US holdings.

indicators.name: Gold (WTI)
indicators.note: Gold dropped nearly 1% — investors moved slightly away from safe-haven assets as midterm uncertainty cleared.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil held near $91 — still elevated given Middle East tensions around Iran.

politics.summary: Western Australia is pushing hard for federal protection of its gas and GST arrangements ahead of a critical Senate vote, the RBA has lifted the cash rate to 4.85%, and Australian creative industries are sounding the alarm over AI copyright laws.

stories.title: WA Premier Roger Cook demands federal hands off gas and GST before Senate vote
stories.why_it_matters: WA Premier Roger Cook is rallying his state's senators to vote as a bloc in an upcoming Senate vote that could affect Western Australia's domestic gas reservation policy and its share of GST revenue. WA has long argued it gets a raw deal from GST distribution, and gas reservation rules are critical to keeping energy affordable for local WA industry. A loss on either front would be a significant blow to WA's economy and to energy-intensive businesses in the state.

stories.title: RBA cash rate hits 4.85% — the big four banks respond
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank of Australia has lifted the official cash rate to 4.85%, and CBA, NAB, Westpac and ANZ have all responded by passing on the increase to borrowers. This means higher mortgage repayments for millions of Australians, further squeezing household budgets. The rate rise signals the RBA is still fighting inflation and isn't done yet — bad news for anyone with a variable rate mortgage, and a continued headwind for consumer spending and the broader economy.

stories.title: Creative industries warn PM over AI copyright laws
stories.why_it_matters: Major figures from Australia's creative industries — musicians, writers, filmmakers — have written to the Prime Minister warning that proposed AI copyright laws could allow tech companies to use their work to train AI models without permission or payment. The AFR also reports that AI firms are separately pressuring musicians to recreate AI-generated tracks specifically to establish copyright claims. It's a growing battle between the tech industry and content creators over who owns the building blocks of the AI economy.

stories.title: Opposition hits PM over accountability concerns
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian is reporting that the opposition is ramping up criticism of the Prime Minister, arguing that a 'protection racket' within government is shielding the PM from scrutiny over policy failures. The article doesn't specify a single incident but reflects a broader political narrative heading into what could be a testing period for the government. The specifics are behind a paywall, but the political temperature in Canberra appears to be rising.

ai.summary: The US midterm results have big implications for AI regulation — Democrats are planning new legislation, AI safety advocates scored wins in key races, and the Claude vs Gemini AI rivalry is heating up with near-identical benchmark scores.

stories.title: AI safety advocates win big after $110 million midterm campaign
stories.why_it_matters: Groups pushing for stronger AI safety rules spent $110 million in the US midterm elections and came out ahead, with several pro-regulation candidates winning key races. With Democrats now controlling Congress and planning AI legislation, this signals that the era of largely unregulated AI development in the US may be coming to an end. For tech companies like Google and Microsoft — both in your portfolio — this means compliance costs and potential constraints on how they can deploy AI products.

stories.title: Democrats plan sweeping AI regulation legislation
stories.why_it_matters: Following their midterm wins, Congressional Democrats are preparing legislation that would regulate artificial intelligence — covering areas like transparency, liability, and potentially limiting certain AI applications. This is the most serious push for federal AI law the US has seen. The big AI companies (Google, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI) are expected to lobby hard, but the political winds have shifted. Expect this debate to dominate tech news over the next two years.

stories.title: Claude vs Gemini: AI rivals separated by just one benchmark point
stories.why_it_matters: A head-to-head comparison of Anthropic's Claude and Google's Gemini AI assistants shows them essentially deadlocked — Claude scores 59 and Gemini 58 on a composite benchmark index. Claude costs $4/month while Gemini costs $20/month, making Claude significantly better value at current performance levels. For Google (GOOG in your portfolio), this shows Gemini is competitive but not yet dominant — the AI assistant race remains very tight.

stories.title: AI giants face regulatory reckoning as Democrats take Congress
stories.why_it_matters: NDTV Profit and others are reporting that the Democratic Congressional win sets up a genuine regulatory reckoning for AI giants including Google, Microsoft, Meta and OpenAI. Areas likely to be targeted include AI-generated content labelling, data privacy, algorithmic accountability, and limits on AI in hiring and healthcare. This isn't necessarily devastating for these companies — regulation can also lock in incumbents — but it adds a new layer of uncertainty and cost to doing business in AI.

sport.summary: The Jillaroos are into the Women's Rugby League World Cup final after beating Fiji 30-14, the Roosters won a nail-biting NRL Grand Final over the Knights 19-18, and Penrith face a fixture headache over their new stadium.

stories.title: Jillaroos into Women's Rugby League World Cup final after beating Fiji 30-14
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's Jillaroos are through to the Women's Rugby League World Cup final after defeating Fiji 30-14 in a game ABC News described as closer than the scoreline suggests at times — hence 'wounded Jillaroos' headlines. The team wasn't at their best but showed plenty of resilience to get the job done. They'll now go into the final as one of the favourites to win the tournament.

stories.title: Roosters win NRL Grand Final over Knights 19-18 in a thriller
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters have claimed the 2026 NRL premiership, defeating the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in a one-point Grand Final at Accor Stadium. It was as tight as it gets — a one-point margin in a grand final is as dramatic as rugby league gets. Full match details are in your NRL draw widget.

stories.title: Penrith face four-round fixture blow over $309m stadium delay
stories.why_it_matters: Penrith are facing a significant disruption, with their new $309 million stadium development creating a four-round fixture headache — meaning the Panthers could be forced to play home games away from Penrith for up to four rounds. For a club that draws much of its strength from home crowd advantage, this is a real competitive disadvantage, not just an inconvenience.

stories.title: Leniu under fire over alleged gesture during Samoa vs opponent clash
stories.why_it_matters: Roosters prop Jared Waerea-Hargreaves' teammate Spencer Leniu is under fire after allegedly making a provocative gesture following a Samoa player being sent to the sin bin during the World Cup. Critics are saying it's not fair conduct and the incident is drawing attention. Disciplinary action could follow, potentially affecting Leniu's availability for future matches.
